# Daily Papers
The project automatically fetches the latest papers from arXiv based on keywords.

The subheadings in the README file represent the search keywords.

Only the most recent articles for each keyword are retained, up to a maximum of 100 papers.

You can click the 'Watch' button to receive daily email notifications.

Last update: 2026-10-19

| **[Velox: Spatial Memory Makes World Models Efficient]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22311v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Video world models turn actions and camera motion into long visual rollouts, making video a natural interface for interactive simulation. Such interaction requires responsive generation, yet coherent rollouts must retain visual memory of what has already been generated. Chunked video diffusion models usually keep this context in growing KV caches, so later chunks become progressively slower. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Velox, a training-free attention router for region-level context selection using frustum slab correspondences from streaming geometry. Velox represents historical blocks as camera frustum slabs with depth intervals and obtains current-block depth through recency-priority multiwarp. For well-covered regions, frustum slab overlap softly modulates each layer's model-derived block importance. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. The fixed token-block granularity matches FlashAttention-style tiled execution and reduces the attention term that grows with rollout length. Frustum slab construction runs asynchronously with denoising on the same H200. At chunk 48, Velox accelerates attention by $4.36\times$ and denoising by $2.43\times$. On the full 158-case WBench navigation split, it remains within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast-Cam. Please see our project page at https://velox-world.com/velox/ for more details.</p></details> |  |
| **[Archer: Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback in Diffusion Language Models]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08086v3)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Diffusion language models (DLMs) can revise earlier predictions as context evolves, but rollback requires costly full-sequence recomputation. Conventional key-value (KV) caching assumes immutable historical states and is difficult to reconcile with such revision. We introduce Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback (Archer), a training-free caching method for rollback-capable DLMs. Archer recomputes the mutable response at every update while reusing prompt K/V within a bounded response-state neighborhood. This asymmetric boundary amortizes prompt computation without restricting rollback. Bounded reuse also delays feedback from tentative tokens while keeping response revision active. Our analysis characterizes the cache boundary, bounds state-dependent approximation error, and gives a decoder-margin condition for preserving full-refresh decisions. On code-generation benchmarks, Archer achieves the best mean performance of 33.63% with a 2.57x mean speedup, reaching 2.95x speedup on a single benchmark. On non-code benchmarks, Archer achieves up to 4.33x speedup over LLaDA-Confidence while improving average accuracy. Controlled analyses support the delayed prompt feedback mechanism. Our code is available at https://github.com/Hxnng/Archer</p></details> | <details><summary>26 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables; revised manuscript...</summary><p>26 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables; revised manuscript, updated author list and affiliations</p></details> |
| **[Efficient KV Cache Migration for Geo-Distributed LLM Inference in Collaborative Edge Computing]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22172v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional capabilities but rely heavily on centralized cloud GPU clusters, leading to high bandwidth costs, latency, and privacy issues. Edge computing offers a solution by deploying LLMs closer to users on edge servers, yet single edge servers often cannot meet LLMs' heavy computational demands. Collaborative Edge Computing (CEC) addresses this challenge by integrating resources of multiple geo-distributed heterogeneous edge servers, which jointly host small model shards and associated Key-Value (KV) cache for distributed inference. However, edge servers may disconnect or easily become overloaded, making it essential to migrate stateful KV cache to other servers for ensuring continuous service. Existing cloud-based KV cache management methods, such as direct cross-GPUs transmission and recomputation from input tokens are ill-suited for bandwidth-constrained and resource-limited edge environments. In this work, we propose EdgeFlow, a novel hybrid KV cache migration scheme that integrates direct KV cache transmission with activation-based recomputation, leveraging parallel computation and communication to minimize migration time. On this basis, we formulate a multi-node KV migration optimization problem and design a 2-approximation algorithm based on improved linear programming relaxation and bipartite graph techniques. Extensive experiments on a real-world distributed LLM inference platform demonstrate that EdgeFlow reduces migration time by up to 45%, significantly enhancing the robustness and efficiency of distributed LLM inference in collaborative edge computing.</p></details> | <details><summary>Accepted by ICDCS 2026...</summary><p>Accepted by ICDCS 2026</p></details> |
| **[DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22130v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.</p></details> | <details><summary>Accepted by NeurIPS 2026...</summary><p>Accepted by NeurIPS 2026</p></details> |
| **[PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01143v4)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, one prompt fans out into $N$ trajectories, yet standard trainers replay the shared prefix's forward and backward pass $N$ times; in long-context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and multimodal workloads, this repetition dominates training compute. Existing designs reuse the prefix within one computation graph (a packed sequence, fused kernel, or tree traversal); under the trainer's memory limits and parallelism, their compute savings do not reliably become shorter steps. We present PrefixFlow, which takes the prefix out of that graph and into the training schedule through a training-time KV cache: Phase A runs one prefix forward and caches its keys and values ($K/V$); Phase B trains suffixes as ordinary microbatches that read only $K/V$ and write back only their gradients ($gK/gV$); Phase C runs one delayed prefix backward on the accumulated $gK/gV$. Memory and parallelism then become manageable: dormant prefix activations are offloaded during Phase B to free high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for suffixes, and context, pipeline, and data parallelism each schedule the phases through a local rule while tensor and expert parallelism need no change, so saved compute becomes shorter steps under any microbatch split. On dense models, and on mixture-of-experts (MoE) models under Rollout Routing Replay, PrefixFlow matches full-sequence training within bfloat16 (BF16) tolerance. Against an identically configured baseline, it speeds up end-to-end verl RL training on a long-prefix RAG workload by $1.90\times$ ($6.1\times$ on the actor update). In controlled sweeps, actor-side speedup grows with prefix ratio and group size, reaching $4.4\times$ at an 83% prefix ratio, while suffix-dominated splits gain little; offloading dormant prefix activations lowers Phase-B peak HBM by up to 59% and extends trainable sequences by $1.66\times$.</p></details> | <details><summary>15 pages. Accepted to the 2026 ACM SIGOPS Annual T...</summary><p>15 pages. Accepted to the 2026 ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (ATC 2026)</p></details> |
| **[Augment the Cache, Replace the Activation: A 2x2 Study of Internal-State Sharing]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22026v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Multi-agent systems built from frozen language models communicate through text, which discards the internal state the sender already computed and makes the receiver pay to rebuild it. Work on internal channels avoids that cost, framing the problem as transfer: agent A sends information to agent B. Every agent pair that must communicate needs its own transfer bridge, and every agent added to a system needs a new bridge fitted against each previous agent. We reframe this problem as sharing: an agent publishes its internal state once into a pool, and every peer reads that pool through a single mechanism fitted to no sender in particular, so adding an agent adds a publisher and no new bridge. Whereas the carrier of the internal state and the fusion mechanism are usually chosen independently in the literature, our main finding is that these two choices are coupled; the deciding factor is where the carrier enters the receiver's computation. Consumability is a property of the receiving computation rather than of the representation. We find that the key-value (KV) cache must be augmented rather than swapped in: the receiver cross-attends over a peer's cache while keeping its own, and with only a small query-side adapter trained, matches the accuracy it gets from reading the source document. Activations invert this. They are best written straight into the receiver, with no bridge, no adapter and no training, which beats exposing them alongside the receiver's own, though that advantage rests on knowing where in the receiver the state belongs. The rule is augment the KV cache, replace the activation, established under one protocol with a shared control ladder. One adapter, trained once, also serves publishers it never trained on, and a pool of several at once, but only those whose internal state lies close to the receiver's own.</p></details> | 10 pages, 2 figures |
| **[Close Enough is Nowhere Near: Fidelity-Consumability Decoupling in KV Caches]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22016v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Multi-agent LLM systems communicate in text, which is lossy and wasteful: the sender throws away the reading it already did. A growing literature instead transmits the KV cache, the natural carrier of that reading. We study the most appealing form of the idea: both models stay frozen and the sender's cache is substituted for the reader's with nothing trained. It does not work, and the obstruction belongs to the reader. A frozen transformer reads only caches close to the one it would have written itself, a region we call its tolerable set. We show that geometric similarity to that cache does not predict whether the reader can use it, and the failure is not gradual, so a more faithful substitute is not the remedy it appears to be. We explain this phenomenon with competitive attention. Experimentally, we test eight diverse substitution methods against two measured anchors: an uninformative cache baseline and the reader's own accuracy from having read the passage. All sit at the baseline. That turns a long tail of separate negative results into one outcome with a stated condition for overturning it. A different design does work: if the reader keeps its own cache and attends over the sender's as extra context, adapting only its queries, it beats its own baseline, and also clears the baseline with eight senders pooled where undirected attention over the same union falls below it. We offer this as a characterization on one probe, not a leaderboard claim. Our central contribution is a redirection: pursuing faithful substitute caches is the wrong target; adding a cache to what the reader already has is the promising one.</p></details> | 10 pages, 3 figures |
| **[KV$^2$: A Self-Refining KV Cache]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03198v2)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>The memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache constrains the practical use of long-context models, and it dominates cost when one prefilled context must later serve many different queries. In this reusable setting, query-agnostic compression trades cost against quality: lightweight estimators are cheap but less accurate, whereas full-context reconstruction scoring is more accurate yet reprocesses the entire prompt. We introduce KV$^2$, a query-agnostic KV-cache compression method based on selective reconstruction. KV$^2$ first uses a lightweight proxy scorer to identify informative in-context tokens, then reprocesses only this subset to compute final eviction scores. On RULER, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongBench, KV$^2$'s margin over baselines widens as the budget tightens: on RULER 16K at a 2% KV-cache budget it improves the average score over the next-best baseline by more than 40 percentage points, and on LongBench it attains the highest average across 2%-10% budgets at lower compression-stage runtime and peak memory than full-context reconstruction. Reusable KV-cache compression thus does not require reprocessing the full context. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/KVsquared-0B97.</p></details> |  |
| **[When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21500v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.</p></details> | <details><summary>9 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables...</summary><p>9 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables</p></details> |
| **[PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21390v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluate it with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets. Results show that PriorityFEC achieves superior task quality over the compared transport schemes, with its advantages becoming particularly pronounced under stringent deadline constraints. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly optimizing KV-cache utility and deadline-aware transport reliability when reusable LLM state must be handed off across unreliable edge networks.</p></details> |  |

| **[The Density of Thought: Predicting and Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21286v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. | **[Range: Decoupling KV-Cache Reuse Granularity from Storage Work]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21241v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>LLM serving reuses cached key-value (KV) state to skip prefill, and growing contexts push that state past GPU HBM and CPU DRAM onto NVMe SSDs, placing prefix restore on the critical path of time-to-first-token (TTFT). This paper presents Range, a KV-cache storage engine for vLLM and LMCache built on one principle: every cost on the storage path scales with bytes or physical batches, never with logical objects. Range tickets replace per-key lookup and ownership with token metadata and physical leases; byte stripes make the on-media layout independent of reuse granularity; completion-owned GPU transfer banks batch delivery and extraction and release each layer to attention as it lands. | **[From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21165v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.</p></details> |  |

| **[Language Models Can Control Their Own Attention]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02737v2)** | 2026-10-14 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Language models spend most of their attention on a small fraction of context, yet they read the entire KV cache to find the few tokens that matter. | **[Accuracy of Uniform Inference on Fine Grid Points]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18627v3)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Uniform confidence bands are widely used in empirical analysis for uncertainty qualification of nonparametric inference of unknown functions. We then derive general upper bounds on the coverage probability and coverage error of uniform confidence bands based on finite-grid multiplier-bootstrap critical values. These bounds distinguish discretization error from the remaining approximation error on the grid. | **[PrefixFlow: Training-Time KV Caching for Schedule-Level Prefix Reuse in LLM RL Training]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01143v4)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, one prompt fans out into $N$ trajectories, yet standard trainers replay the shared prefix's forward and backward pass $N$ times; in long-context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and multimodal workloads, this repetition dominates training compute. Memory and parallelism then become manageable: dormant prefix activations are offloaded during Phase B to free high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for suffixes, and context, pipeline, and data parallelism each schedule the phases through a local rule while tensor and expert parallelism need no change, so saved compute becomes shorter steps under any microbatch split. | **[Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22370v1)** | 2026-10-15 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence. In this work, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the underlying diffusion dynamics. Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information. To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics- aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised estimate. The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details. Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates. Experiments on PixArt-a and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungJuCha/DaTMe.</p></details> | <details><summary>Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com...</summary><p>Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. They perform hard caching: the signal is a binary switch between refresh and reuse, and every step, fresh or cached, advances by the prescribed step size. We observe that the signal carries much more than this switch. How far it sits below the threshold, its headroom, predicts the error induced by reuse. We propose SoftCache, which performs soft caching: instead of a binary switch, the headroom sets how far each cached step goes. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Our experiments show agents coordinating across roles and adapting their decisions to market feedback. Our key observation is that a WAM can indeed autoregressively regenerate complete rollouts of previously learned tasks and replay them to mitigate forgetting. However, replaying such raw rollouts still lags far behind replaying real data, which we attribute to two issues. First, the WAM is unable to recognize task completion and keeps generating purposeless motion after the task is done. Second, under open-loop generation, the generated actions gradually drift away from the generated observations. | **[Hierarchical Curriculum Learning for Surgical Video Generation: Focusing on Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach Robotic Thyroidectomy Datasets]( https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17684v1)** | 2026-10-13 | <details><summary>Show</summary><p>High-fidelity surgical video generation is increasingly important for surgical education, simulation, and downstream AI training, as conventional simulation pipelines are limited by cost, realism, and scenario diversity.
